title: Count islands in a grid
prompt: Implement numIslands(grid [][]byte) int: how many groups of '1' cells are connected up, down, left or right. You may write over the grid.
explanation: Counting islands is counting how many times you have to start a flood fill. Overwriting each visited '1' with water is the visited set, so it costs no extra memory and the outer loop cannot count the same island twice.
hints: When the outer scan lands on land, walk that whole island before moving on.
Sink what you visit (write water over it) so it is never counted again.

title: Kth largest with a size-k heap
prompt: Implement findKthLargest(nums []int, k int) int without sorting the whole slice. A minHeap type (container/heap ready) is already compiled in; import "container/heap" and use heap.Push/heap.Pop on &minHeap{}.
explanation: Sorting is n log n and throws away the fact that k is small. Keeping only k candidates in a min-heap makes its root the kth largest by construction: push everything, pop whenever the heap grows past k, and the cost is n log k.
hints: Only k numbers can ever matter; the smallest of those is the one to throw away.
If the smallest survivor is the answer, the heap you want is ordered smallest first.

title: All subsets
prompt: Implement subsets(nums []int) [][]int: every subset of a slice of distinct ints, in any order. The empty subset counts.
explanation: Subsets is the plainest backtracking shape: at index i, recurse without nums[i], then with it, and undo the choice on the way out. Recording a copy matters because cur is reused; appending cur itself would leave every answer pointing at the same array.
hints: Each element is one yes/no decision, so the recursion branches twice and needs no loop.
Snapshot the working slice when you record it, or later pushes will rewrite answers you already saved.

title: Rotate a square matrix in place
prompt: Implement rotate(matrix [][]int): turn an n x n matrix 90 degrees clockwise, in place. No second grid.
explanation: A clockwise rotation is a transpose followed by reversing each row. The transpose loop starts at c = r+1 so every pair is swapped once; starting from 0 swaps each pair twice and leaves the grid exactly as it was.
hints: Two cheap passes over the same memory beat one clever pass, and beat allocating a second grid.
Mirror across the top-left to bottom-right diagonal first, then flip each row end to end.

title: Can you reach the last index
prompt: Implement canJump(nums []int) bool: from index 0, nums[i] is the most you may jump forward from i. Can you land on the last index? One pass.
explanation: Greedy is safe here because only the furthest index you could be standing on matters, never the path that got you there. If the scan ever arrives at an index past that furthest point, nothing earlier could have covered it.
hints: Carry one number: the furthest index still within your grasp so far.
The answer is false the moment the loop steps past that number, and true if it never does.

title: Count the set bits
prompt: Implement hammingWeight(n uint32) int: how many bits of n are 1. No math/bits, no strconv, and try to make the loop run once per set bit rather than 32 times.
explanation: Subtracting one flips the lowest set bit to zero and turns every zero below it into a one, so and-ing the two together removes exactly that bit. The loop then costs one step per one-bit instead of one per bit of width.
hints: Shifting 32 times works, but there is a trick that costs one step per one-bit.
Look at what n-1 does to the lowest one and to everything under it, then combine the two values.
